extracted.intended_audience: experimental scientists, physicists/chemists, and students of physical science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for designing measurements, comparing experimental results with theory, diagnosing discordances, and choosing or weighing different modes of measurement in physical science. Covers error analysis, method selection, and how to treat residual discrepancies as potential discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare means with effect present vs absent
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the mean of observations when the effect to be measured is present and compare it with the mean of the remainder in which the effect is absent (or acts in opposite direction); the difference represents the amount of the effect (or double the amount respectively).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trusting chance that other effects will neutralise themselves in drawing each mean is acceptable, but it is a great advantage to decide by theory when each principal disturbing effect is present or absent so that means may be drawn to separate each such effect. Example: atmospheric tides — compare means when the moon was on the meridian vs on the horizon. If there are several principal effects, draw means giving different sums so as to create simultaneous equations to solve for each quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use probable error of the mean to assess agreement with theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate the probable error of the mean of the observed results and observe whether the theoretical result falls within the limits of probable error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the theoretical result lies within the limits and experimental results agree with each other, the probability of the theory is much increased. Remember probable error measures incidental and variable errors only and does not indicate fixed causes of error; non-overlapping probable-error limits between two modes implies overlooked fixed error(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification by precise theoretical prediction and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory test of a theory is its application to predict precise quantities of phenomena which can then be measured; repeated deductive calculations each ending in verification strengthen the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Newton's successive deductions comparing predicted quantities (moon fall, tidal motions) with observations. Use accurate instruments and repeated comparison; successive confirmations increase confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize degrees of verification and method accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative verification is a matter of degree and probability; a less accurate method cannot verify a more accurate one, and when several distinct modes produce results, it can be delicate to decide which is most reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the most accurate methods for establishing standards; use less accurate or indirect methods for derived quantities. Example: Laplace's inference of planetary ellipticity vs direct micrometrical measurements; Rankine's theoretical estimate of specific heat later verified by Regnault's improved experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four possible explanations for discordance between theory and experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: When a distinct want of accordance exists between theory and direct measurement, the discrepancy may be due to: (1) experimental casual error; (2) inaccurate constant numbers or quantitative data used in theory; (3) the theory's mathematical form being incorrect; (4) an unknown regular cause producing a residual effect (possible new phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this diagnostic list as an organizing principle for investigation; no precise rule exists for which case applies—experimenter's insight required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic procedure for investigating discrepancies
rubrics_metrics.description: If experimental measurements are few, repeat them to increase accuracy (probable accuracy increases as square root of number). If unchanged, change apparatus/materials/procedure to remove constant errors; if still discrepant, invent widely different modes of measurement to avoid common errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try five or six essentially different modes if possible. If discrepancy persists, review the data used in theoretical calculations and repeat/modify those measurements too. This is the recommended escalation: more repeats → apparatus/procedure variation → independent methods → reevaluation of theoretical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate hypotheses by wider consistency, not just fit to few results
rubrics_metrics.description: Never estimate the probability of an hypothesis merely by its accordance with a few results; consider its general analogy and accordance with other known laws and absence of conflict with other probable theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good hypothesis should admit deduction of facts verified in observation across many ways; prefer hypotheses that reconcile broader sets of phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat persistent unexplained residuals as new empirical facts
rubrics_metrics.description: If measurements are accurate and theory probable yet discrepancy remains, regard the residual as an empirical fact potentially indicating a new cause or phenomenon worthy of further investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outstanding residual discrepancies have often led to important discoveries; record and investigate rather than force reconciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select measurement mode by theory-based leverage and practical trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: When theory links quantities, measure the fundamental quantity that can be determined most precisely and use theory to derive others; select the mode of measurement that is most accurate or, where acceptable, most convenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: chemists choose compounds allowing most accurate atomic-weight analysis; in hygrometry choose between chemical absorption (most accurate but troublesome) and wet/dry-bulb thermometers (sufficiently exact and convenient for meteorological work). Consider the relation of quantities (atomic weight, atomic volume, atomic heat) to exploit shared information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use agreement of distinct independent methods as strong confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Close accordance between results from entirely different methods should be regarded as the best possible proof of approximate correctness of the mean result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nevertheless, remain cautious: new methods have sometimes disclosed previously hidden discrepancies. Use multiple independent modes (e.g., velocity of light by astronomical aberration, transit timings, and laboratory experiments) to detect reduction errors or overlooked data.

rubrics_metrics.name: When methods disagree, weigh method quality and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: In conflicts among determinations, scrutinize probable errors, independence of methods, quality of reductions, and recency/care of experiments; more careful recent methods may warrant rejecting earlier results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: differing estimates of solar parallax and earth's density led to re-discussion of older reductions and preference for newer corrected values. Consider repeating classical experiments with improved techniques if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative aggregation and uncertainty assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate multiple determinations (simple mean, mean error, probable error) to estimate the best guess and bounds for the true value; increasing number of experiments reduces casual error as square root of N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that simple aggregation treats determinations equally — where newer/careful experiments lie outside earlier error bounds, re-evaluate weighting and consider discarding obsolete results. Use statistical measures to express likelihood that the truth lies within given bounds.
